Antigen. An antigen is any foreign molecule or substance that triggers an immune response by binding to antibodies or being recognized by immune cells. Antigens are typically proteins, polysaccharides, or nucleic acids present on pathogen surfaces, toxins, or allergens. Their recognition initiates the adaptive immune system's cascade of B-cell and T-cell activation, forming the cornerstone of immunological defense and vaccination.

The term antigen derives from "antibody generator"—any molecule that provokes antibody production is, by definition, an antigen. Most antigens are proteins or protein-polysaccharide complexes. The immune system recognizes specific three-dimensional regions of the antigen called epitopes, or antigenic determinants, which serve as the lock for antibody binding.

Antigens must be foreign to the body—present on invading pathogens, viruses, toxins, or pollen—or abnormal, such as tumor-associated proteins on cancer cells. The immune system normally ignores self-antigens through a process called tolerance. Blood group antigens, like ABO types, are glycoproteins on red blood cell surfaces. These are inherited and determine transfusion compatibility because mismatched antigens trigger severe immune reactions.

Major histocompatibility complex, or MHC, molecules present antigens to T cells. MHC class I presents intracellular antigens from viruses, while MHC class II presents extracellular antigens from pathogens to different T-cell subsets. The specificity of immune recognition is extraordinary—antibodies can distinguish between antigens that differ by a single amino acid or sugar. This specificity is why the immune system can respond to millions of distinct pathogens.

Allergens are antigens that trigger inappropriate, or IgE-mediated, immune responses in sensitive individuals. Examples include pollen, peanut proteins, and dust-mite fecal matter, which are harmless but provoke histamine release and inflammation.
